transcript.text: Good morning. Most of you have used an online translator at some point, and perhaps you've been impressed, or amused, by the result. Today I want to explain how these systems work and where they still fail.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: Translation is a good example of how artificial intelligence affects everyday life. Millions of people use it every day to read websites, talk to hotel staff abroad or help with homework, often without thinking about the technology behind it.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: Modern systems are called neural systems. When you enter a sentence, the first step is that it is split into small units called tokens, which may be whole words or parts of words.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: The reason for this step is practical. A computer cannot work directly with letters and words in the way that people do, so everything has to be turned into a form that can be calculated, and splitting text into smaller pieces makes the vocabulary more manageable.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: Second, each token is converted into a list of numbers. These numbers capture something about its meaning, so that words with similar meanings have similar numbers.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: Third, the model calculates which words in the sentence are related to each other. In a long sentence, a pronoun at the end may refer to a noun at the beginning, and the system must keep track of that connection.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: This stage is where modern systems made their biggest advance. Earlier methods could only look at a few words at a time, so they often produced sentences that were grammatical at the start but strange by the end.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: Finally, the system generates the translation one word at a time, each time choosing the most likely next word given everything it has already produced.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: The process is repeated until the system produces a signal that the sentence is complete. Because of the way it works, the same input can sometimes give slightly different translations, which surprises many users.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: The history is interesting. The first public demonstration, in nineteen fifty-four, translated about sixty Russian sentences into English, and the organisers predicted the problem would be solved within five years.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: In fact it took decades. Until the two thousand and tens, most systems used statistics, matching phrases found in millions of existing translations. Neural systems arrived around two thousand and sixteen and produced a sudden jump in quality.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: The improvement was so sudden that many professional translators were surprised. Some of them feared for their jobs, though in practice the demand for human translators has stayed fairly stable, because customers still want a person to take responsibility for the final text.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: Still, there are limits. Systems struggle with languages that have little written material online, such as many African languages, because there's not enough data to learn from.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: They also have trouble with idioms and humour. A system might translate 'it's raining cats and dogs' word for word, producing nonsense. For this reason, professional translators still check important documents.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: My advice, if you use these tools, is to treat them as a first draft. Read the result carefully, check any names and numbers, and ask a speaker of the language if the text really matters, for example in a contract or a medical document.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL

transcript.text: So machine translation is a powerful tool but not a replacement for human judgement. Thank you for listening.
transcript.speaker: DR VOGEL
